street_smart.title: You're riding your two-wheeler on a narrow road when a water tanker overtakes way too close and swerves back in before it's fully past you — like today's Varthur case where a tanker driver nearly mowed down a biker and was arrested. What do you do in that moment and right after?
street_smart.based_on: Today's real Bengaluru incident: a tanker driver was arrested after nearly mowing down a biker in Bengaluru's Varthur (Deccan Herald). Heavy-vehicle blind-spot road safety hasn't been used as a street-smart topic in the last three weeks — recent transport-safety scenarios covered a Metro queue punch-up (Aug 14), an underpass cave-in (Aug 11), and a traffic-cop assault (Aug 17/18), all different mechanisms from a heavy vehicle squeezing a two-wheeler off the road.
street_smart.situation: The tanker is still moving, the road is narrow, and other traffic is backed up behind you both.

choices.text: Brake and drop back to get clear of the tanker's blind spot rather than riding alongside or behind it, then once you're safely stopped, note its registration number, time, and location, and report it to the police (100) or the traffic police's public complaint channel.
choices.feedback: Correct — heavy vehicles like tankers have large blind spots, especially on the left and rear, so the real fix is getting out of that zone first. Reporting the plate number afterwards is exactly what let police trace and arrest today's Varthur driver — not a roadside confrontation.

choices.text: Speed up, cut in front of the tanker, and block it so you can get out and argue with the driver about the near-miss.
choices.feedback: This is the trap — putting yourself directly in front of or beside a multi-tonne vehicle to make a point is exactly how near-misses turn fatal. Tanker and truck drivers often have limited visibility and much longer stopping distances, so confrontation at close range multiplies the risk instead of resolving it.

choices.text: Stop right where you are, still close to the tanker, to snap a photo of its number plate before it drives off.
choices.feedback: Recording evidence is the right instinct, but stopping in the tanker's path or blind spot to do it recreates the exact danger you just escaped. Pull well clear first, then note the plate.

choices.text: Ride on without reporting it, since nothing actually happened to you.
choices.feedback: Understandable, but unreported near-misses let dangerous driving continue unchecked. A quick report with the registration number — even after the fact — helps build a record, as it did in today's case where the driver was traced and arrested.

takeaways: Never ride alongside or directly behind a large vehicle like a tanker or bus — stay out of its blind spots, especially on the left and rear.

If a heavy-vehicle driver is genuinely dangerous, don't confront them directly — pull clear first, then note the registration number and report it to the police (100) or the traffic police's complaint channel.
A near-miss is still worth reporting — it builds a record that can lead to action, as it did in today's Varthur case.

quiz.question: From September 1, what will Kempegowda International Airport's User Development Fee be for departing passengers, per today's report?
quiz.why: A UDF is a charge airports levy directly on passengers to help fund airport infrastructure and operations, separate from the airline's own ticket price.

quiz.question: Karnataka's H1N1 (swine flu) case count has crossed what number, per today's report?
quiz.why: H1N1 is a seasonal flu strain that typically spikes in India during and just after the monsoon months.

quiz.question: A Bengaluru consumer court ordered a firm to pay how much after a customer's number plate arrived a year late, per today's report?
quiz.why: Consumer commissions (under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019) handle complaints about defective goods or delayed/deficient service, and you don't need a lawyer to file one.

quiz.question: Bengaluru draws most of its municipal drinking water from which river, pumped in from about 100km away?
quiz.why: The Cauvery Water Supply Scheme lifts water from the river near Torekadanahalli (T.K. Halli) and pumps it uphill into the city — one of the most energy-intensive water supply systems in the country.

quiz.question: In which year was the Reserve Bank of India established?
quiz.why: The RBI started as a privately-held institution under the RBI Act, 1934, and was nationalised only in 1949.
